name: The Andrus household — a name from the post office's letter lists
head: andrus_thomas

arrival.note: A BOUND FROM THE RETURN, NOT AN ARRIVAL. The office's list of letters uncalled-for is a RETURN — its statement of what was still unclaimed on ONE day — and the paper reprinted one return over as many consecutive issues as it took, so the bound is dated by the return of March 1835 and not by the issue it was read in (T-0425). The earliest issue this project reads the name in is 1835-05-20, 50 days later; that gap is an accident of which impression an extraction pass reached, and it is not evidence. Somebody was writing to this name at Chicago by 1835-03-31 and at no stated time before it; nothing says when they came. The date lines the printings set, and how they were weighed, stand beside this rule in tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py.

arrival_year.note: A STATED YEAR, AND THE DRAW IT CORRECTS. The completed resident-research pass on andrus_thomas read a DuPage history as giving his arrival at Chicago on 1 December 1833, carpenter and pile-driving work through 1834, a return east in the autumn of 1834 and an arrival back at Chicago in June 1835 before he settled in DuPage. The year written here is the FIRST arrival, which is what this field asks for. The going and returning is a chronology no field on this card carries and it is not asserted here; the household's `arrival` block keeps its own bound of 1835-03-31 from the Chicago Democrat, which the June 1835 return does not contradict. Under the evidence ladder ratified 2026-09-03 a source earlier than 1 July 1835 corroborates and dates and never promotes: the person's grade does not move on this.

origin.note: DRAWN FROM A SURVIVORSHIP SAMPLE. No source says where this household came from. The region is drawn from the birthplaces of the seventy Old Settlers who registered an arrival at or before 1835 — a self-selected roll set down forty-four years later that over-represents the men who stayed and prospered, as the town model's own open questions say. It is the only origin distribution this project holds and this value is drawn from it, not measured.

reason_for_coming.value: The building of a town three years old
reason_for_coming.note: ARGUED FROM THIS HOUSEHOLD'S OWN RECORDED TRADE, WHICH IS NOT ITS MOTIVE. The head is recorded as carpenter, and this names the documented draw that trade answered in this town in this decade. It does not claim to know why these people came. Which of these draws brought this household is not recorded, and no committed source apportions the town between them.

last_dated_appearance.note: A DATED READING OF THIS PERSON, AND THE LAST ONE THE CORPUS HOLDS. Read from `profile_facts` as `1835-07-01`, which reaches 1835-07-01 — a window that covers 1835-07-01 itself, so it pins no last sighting before the day and cannot be read as one. THE FIELD IS THE EVIDENCE UNDER THE VERDICT, not a new claim: nothing here moves the presence off `uncertain`, and T-1159 and T-1172 classify this household by this date instead of reading it out of the prose (T-1144 acceptance 9).

present_on_scene_date.note: THE CORPUS STOPS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE. Nothing after 1835-05-20 follows this person to 1 July 1835 or says they left. `uncertain` rather than dropped — the distinction index.json draws for Jeremiah Porter, and a finding, not a gap.

persons.name: Thomas Andrus

occupation.note: T-0485: independently corroborated resident research. DuPage history gives a detailed chronology for Thomas Andrus: arrival in Chicago Dec. 1, 1833, carpenter/pile-driving work in 1834, return east in autumn 1834, and arrival back at Chicago in June 1835 before settling in DuPage in July. This independently identifies the exact person behind the regional postal seed.

persons.note: INDEPENDENTLY CORROBORATED RESIDENT. Originally documented in Chicago post-office evidence; independent resident research now corroborates the identity. KNOWN ONLY FROM THE POST OFFICE, IN ONE RETURN. The papers print 'Andrus, Tomas' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 20 May 1835, column 13 — dated 1835-05-20. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (docs/LIBERTIES.md L214), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py). No figure is drawn (L1).

refusals.reason: This card rests on 1 thing(s) the consolidation did not read — rr_dupage_andrus_1882. G3 fired on the seven domains the ladder reads and says nothing about the evidence outside them, so the grade stands. The same reasoning the ladder's own G5 gives for abstaining (T-0515).

profile_facts.note: The DuPage history gives a day, and the household's own arrival block is explicit that its 1835-03-31 is a BOUND FROM THE RETURN and not an arrival. The two are different claims about different things and both stand; the bound is not touched.

roles.note: THE BOUND IS THE SOURCE'S, NOT THE MAN'S. This role is carried by the card's 1835 occupation block and is dated by what the cited source or sources are ABOUT, which is why `precision` can be no better than the span they cover. The span reaches 1835, so this role stands in the scene-date view. The printing the trade was read off is not on the card and is fetched by T-1254.

basis.note: Drawn from the 1840 Chicago schedule's column 'free white males 15 under 20', one of its male bands, conditioned on `named_on_a_roll_15_and_over` because the person is named in their own right on any other roll this layer was minted from - a letter list, a subscription, a court docket, a trade notice - or carries a role, a trade, a marriage or a parenthood.

replaceable_by.match: a source that states this person's age, their birth year, or an interval either can be read out of

age_band.note: AN AGE BAND, NEVER A YEAR. No source this project holds bears on when this person was born, so the band is drawn from the only committed sex by age distribution the project has - the 1840 Chicago schedule, five years after the scene and a town twice the size - seeded by this person's own id ('andrus_thomas:age_bands_1840'). AND THE CONDITIONING IS THE MODEL'S, NOT A SOURCE'S: that a roll naming a person in their own right names somebody 15 or over. The 1840 schedule counts a child as a tally inside a household and never as a correspondent; 15 rather than 20 because an apprentice or a journeyman stands on a trade roll. No source states this rule. No exact year is written, because a year drawn from a decadal band would read as a record of a birth.

sex_basis.note: A FORENAME THAT STANDS IN ONE SEX'S NAMING ONLY. 'Thomas' is read as male because 2 persons in this layer whose sex a source records bear it (church_thomas, owen_thomas_jv), and it stands in the irish male forename pool of this town's own attested naming. Nothing about this person is recorded; the name is the whole of the reasoning, and the table that licenses it — data/research/residents/forename_sex.json — refuses a name its own evidence splits, refuses Jean, Marion, Leslie and Francis by name, and refuses an initial outright.

research_note: MINTED FROM THE LETTER LISTS (T-0378, T-0379). THE HOUSEHOLD IS A CONTAINER, NOT AN ARGUMENT: every other record here argues for a household, and this one argues for a PERSON. `data/residents/` cannot carry a person outside a household, so one was written around them and told to claim nothing — one member, no dwelling, no division, no trade, no family, no arrival beyond the paper's bound. tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py derives the set and prints every refusal, `--gate` proves no record here gained a roof, a trade or a second member, and docs/LIBERTIES.md L214 carries the change of scale.
